summary: Sirach 25 gathers several wisdom sayings about agreement, aging, happiness, and the fear of the Lord. The chapter then turns sharply to warnings about a wicked woman, using severe comparisons and household language that reflects an ancient patriarchal setting. Verse 12 is blank in the World English Bible, so the movement passes directly from the fear of the Lord in verse 11 to the sayings that begin in verse 13.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows Sirach's wisdom instruction at both its attractive and difficult edges: it praises harmony, counsel, experience, and reverence for God, while also preserving harsh gendered counsel that readers must handle with historical distance. It also illustrates the book's habit of arranging memorable lists and comparisons for moral formation.

context.author: Yeshua (Jesus) son of Eleazar son of Sira, a Jerusalem teacher and scribe; his unnamed grandson later translated the Hebrew book into Greek in Egypt.
context.audience: Students seeking disciplined wisdom in Jerusalem, and later Greek-reading Jews who wanted instruction for living according to the law.
context.date: The Hebrew work was composed in the early second century BC, likely around 180–175 BC; the Greek translation followed after the grandson came to Egypt, commonly understood as 132 BC.
context.setting: Jerusalem under Hellenistic rule, with temple worship, scribal study, and Greek-speaking Mediterranean culture forming the world around the book.
context.literaryForm: Wisdom instruction: compact poetic sayings, lists, comparisons, and practical counsel for ordinary life.

outline.heading: Three Things Loved and Three Hated
outline.note: The chapter opens with two lists: harmonious relationships are called beautiful, while arrogant poverty, lying wealth, and adulterous old age are rejected.

outline.heading: Wisdom in Old Age
outline.note: Aging is honored when it carries gathered experience, judgment, counsel, wisdom, and the fear of the Lord.

outline.heading: The Happy and the Greatest
outline.note: The teacher lists people counted happy, then places finding wisdom under the greater measure of fearing the Lord.

outline.heading: A Blank Verse in This Edition
outline.note: The World English Bible leaves verse 12 blank.

outline.heading: Wounds, Enemies, and a Wicked Woman
outline.note: The chapter turns to intense comparisons, setting wounds, enemies, venom, and malice beside the misery attributed to a wicked woman.

outline.heading: Household Warnings
outline.note: The final sayings warn against beauty, describe household shame and sorrow, connect sin and death to a woman, and end with commands about controlling or separating from a wicked woman.

keyVerses.text: I enjoy three things, and they are beautiful before the Lord and men: the agreement of kindred, the friendship of neighbors, and a woman and her husband who walk together in agreement.
keyVerses.why: This verse anchors the chapter's positive opening: agreement among relatives, neighbors, and spouses is presented as socially and religiously beautiful.

keyVerses.text: Much experience is the crown of the aged. Their glory is the fear of the Lord.
keyVerses.why: This sums up the chapter's praise of old age when it is joined to experience and reverence for God.

keyVerses.text: The fear of the Lord surpasses all things. To whom shall he who holds it be likened?
keyVerses.why: This is the high point of the chapter's wisdom scale, placing fear of the Lord above the happy conditions listed before it.

keyVerses.text: The beginning of sin came from a woman. Because of her, we all die.
keyVerses.why: This is one of the chapter's hardest sayings, and it signals how strongly the final section links women, sin, and death in its ancient male-voiced instruction.

themes: fear of the Lord above all
harsh counsel about a wicked woman

questions.question: Why does the chapter begin with things the speaker enjoys and hates?
questions.answer: The opening uses paired lists to sharpen moral perception. Verse 1 names three forms of agreement that are beautiful before the Lord and people, while verse 2 names three kinds of conduct the speaker says his soul hates. The contrast prepares the reader to think in vivid categories of wise and foolish life.

questions.question: What does “agreement” mean in this chapter?
questions.answer: In verse 1, agreement appears in relationships: kindred, neighbors, and a woman with her husband. The word points to harmony or walking together rather than mere absence of conflict. The chapter treats such agreement as publicly and religiously beautiful.

questions.question: Is the chapter saying all old people are wise?
questions.answer: No. Verse 2 criticizes “an old fool who is an adulterer,” while verses 4-6 praise judgment, counsel, wisdom, understanding, experience, and fear of the Lord in the aged. The chapter honors old age when it has become formed by wisdom, not simply because time has passed.

questions.question: Why does verse 3 ask about youth and old age?
questions.answer: Verse 3 assumes that old age does not automatically produce what was never gathered earlier. In the flow of the chapter, youth is the time to acquire what later becomes judgment, counsel, and experience. The saying is practical rather than biographical; it warns against postponing formation.

questions.question: What is “the fear of the Lord” doing here?
questions.answer: The phrase appears in verses 6, 10, and 11 as the chapter's highest measure of wisdom. In Sirach this phrase means practiced allegiance and reverence for God, not panic. In this chapter it is the aged person's glory and something greater even than finding wisdom.

questions.question: Why is verse 12 empty?
questions.answer: The World English Bible leaves verse 12 blank. Sirach survives in different textual forms, and editions can differ in wording and verse numbering. Other editions may include additional lines or number the passage differently.

questions.question: Why does the chapter speak so harshly about a wicked woman?
questions.answer: Verses 13-26 preserve severe household warnings from an ancient male teacher's setting. The text does not speak neutrally about women here; it uses sweeping comparisons and commands that reflect patriarchal suspicion and household power. Responsible readers differ on how to weigh these sayings, but the first step is to name what the chapter says without turning it into timeless neutral psychology.

questions.question: Does verse 24 refer to Eve?
questions.answer: Verse 24 says, “The beginning of sin came from a woman. Because of her, we all die.” It does not name Eve, but many later readers connect the line with the Genesis story. Since the verse itself does not spell out the reference, it is better to say that the chapter links woman, sin, and death, while later interpretation often reads Eve in the background.

questions.question: Should the command to “cut her away from your flesh” be read as a modern instruction?
questions.answer: Verse 26 belongs to the chapter's ancient household counsel about a wicked woman who does not go as directed. It should not be lifted out as a direct modern policy or permission for harm. The chapter depicts a patriarchal power arrangement, and any ethical application has to reckon with that distance.

glossary.def: Harmony or walking together in a relationship; verse 1 uses it for kindred and for a woman and her husband.
Wise discernment or sound decision-making; verse 4 calls it beautiful in the gray-haired.
Careful practical wisdom; verse 9 counts a person happy who has found it.
Reverent allegiance to God expressed in a wise life; in this chapter it is the aged person's glory and surpasses all things.
The repeated figure in the chapter's final warnings, where household misery and danger are described through harsh gendered sayings.
